## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 8 (*Tirokuṭṭuccārachaḍḍana*) is the eighth expiation rule for Buddhist nuns in the Pali Vinaya Piṭaka [SuttaCentral]. It establishes that a nun who throws or disposes of feces, urine, rubbish, or food scraps over a wall or fence (*tirokudde vā tiropākāre vā*) commits an offense requiring confession (*pācittiya*) [SuttaCentral; Bechert et al. 1997; Hüsken 1997]. Unlike certain monastic regulations concerning bodily evacuation, this rule primarily governs sanitary waste disposal [Bechert et al. 1997]. As scholars note, nuns living in settlement-adjacent dwellings were subject to intense lay scrutiny, creating an urgent need for waste management guidelines that directly complement Cullavagga regulations [Hüsken 1997]. The commentary (*Samantapāsādikā*) notes that while no explicit pācittiya counterpart exists for monks, identical conduct on their part constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) [Hüsken 1997]. Furthermore, the non-offense clause (*anāpatti*) exempts a nun who looks beforehand (*oloketvā*) to ensure that the refuse does not strike a passerby on the head [Hüsken 1997].

The rule is closely related to the succeeding rule, Pācittiya 9, which shifts the prohibited disposal site from over a wall to onto green ground or crops (*harite*) [Hüsken 1997]. Text-reuse analysis by DharmaNexus confirms that Pācittiya 8 shares extensive formulaic material with Pācittiya 9 (§1.18–2.1.12), along with numerous other Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga rules [DharmaNexus]. Parallels to the rule are attested widely across early Vinaya traditions: corresponding rules appear in the Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādin Bhikṣuṇī Vinaya (where it corresponds to Pc 138), as well as in the Dharmaguptaka, Mahīśāsaka, Sarvāstivāda, and Mūlasarvāstivāda traditions preserved in Chinese and Tibetan recensions, alongside internal Pali parallels in the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha and the Parivāra [SuttaCentral; Bechert et al. 1997; DharmaNexus]. English translations of the rule include that of Bhikkhu Brahmali [SuttaCentral].
